paper.title: Comprehensive Robustness Analysis of LiDAR-based 3D Object Detection in Autonomous Driving

read: full text: Sections 1-5 including sensitivity analysis and limitations; appendix (attack formulas, budgets, training configs, extra density plots) not available in the extracted text

claims.claim: Whether a LiDAR 3D object detector withstands adversarial point-cloud attacks depends on how it encodes the point cloud: detectors that voxelise the scene in 3D, legacy or recent, are far more vulnerable to attacks that shift point coordinates or corrupt intermediate features than detectors that collapse the scene into vertical pillars, while pillar-based detectors are instead the ones vulnerable to injected points. Supported only if, on both a 32-beam and a 64-beam driving dataset, the relative AP drop under a coordinate-perturbation attack and under a feature-space attack is larger for each of two voxel-based detectors than for each of two pillar-based detectors, for both cars and safety-critical classes (pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists); if under a point-injection attack the relative car AP drop is larger for each pillar-based detector than for each voxel-based one on both datasets; and if a black-box attack not tailored to any architecture costs every detector less than 3% AP.
claims.decision_rule: PB and NE AP drop: both voxel > both pillar on cars and safety-critical, nuScenes and Waymo; PA car drop: both pillar > both voxel on both datasets; LiDAttack drop < 3% everywhere.

claims.claim: For voxel-based LiDAR 3D detectors, denser point clouds do not protect against attacks that shift point coordinates: the extra geometric detail gives the attacker more to manipulate. Supported only if, for both voxel-based detectors tested, the relative car AP drop under a coordinate-perturbation attack and under a feature-space attack is larger on a dataset recorded with a 64-beam LiDAR than on one recorded with a 32-beam LiDAR; if under these attacks the attack success rate on objects within 20 m of the vehicle is not lower than on objects 35-50 m away; and if at least some model-attack pairs show attack success that does not fall as the number of points on the object rises.
claims.decision_rule: Voxel detectors: PB and NE car AP drop Waymo > nuScenes; near-object ASR not lower than far under PB/NE; density-invariant or inverse ASR for some pairs.

experiments.text: Choose detectors that separate encoder type from recency and train them to parity. Setup: two pillar-based detectors (PointPillars with an anchor head; PillarNeSt with a ConvNeXt backbone and centre-based head) and two voxel-based detectors (CenterPoint with a centre heatmap head; FocalFormer3D with a transformer head built to reduce false negatives); evaluate on nuScenes (32-beam) and Waymo (64-beam), using released weights where they exist and otherwise training from scratch in mmdetection3d. Clean mAP: PointPillars 35.9 / 58.4, PillarNeSt 66.9 / 66.2, CenterPoint 58.0 / 67.8, FocalFormer3D 70.5 / 71.9 (nuScenes / Waymo).

Choose LiDAR-specific attacks so every architecture faces at least one aimed at its weakness, and define success honestly. Setup: a white-box attack that minimises the detector's class-probability-times-IoU confidence in three modes, adding points (affects depth, expected to hurt pillars), removing points (affects density, expected to hurt heatmap heads) and shifting point coordinates (expected to hurt voxels); a white-box feature-space attack that suppresses high-contribution and amplifies low-contribution feature-map entries; and a black-box genetic simulated-annealing attack with tight point-distance constraints. Count an attack as successful on an object only if the object was detected on the clean cloud and is then misclassified or kept with confidence below 0.15. Report relative AP drop and relative confidence drop for cars and for safety-critical classes. A sensitivity check shows average success flat between thresholds 0.10 and 0.15 and within 0.02 of the standard success definition at 0.15 on Waymo.

Measure AP loss for every detector, attack, class group and dataset. Result (relative AP drop, %): under coordinate shifts, voxel detectors lose 65.5 and 38.9 on nuScenes cars and 91.0 and 88.5 on Waymo cars (CenterPoint, FocalFormer3D) against 20.2 and 10.0, and 18.6 and 9.4, for the pillar detectors (PillarNeSt, PointPillars), with the same ordering for safety-critical classes (e.g. Waymo 96.3 and 61.1 vs 13.8 and 15.8). Under the feature-space attack voxel detectors lose 82.0 and 82.1 on Waymo cars against 12.8 and 7.1. Under point injection the ordering reverses for cars: pillar detectors lose 32.2 and 85.4 on nuScenes and 24.0 and 57.5 on Waymo against 3.9 and 7.8, and 0.0 and 8.0, for voxel detectors. For safety-critical classes it does not fully reverse (Waymo: CenterPoint 25.3 vs PillarNeSt 24.5). PillarNeSt, despite a centre heatmap head like CenterPoint's, resists the feature-space attack.

Check that the vulnerabilities are specific to structured perturbations rather than to any input change. Setup: the black-box genetic attack, not biased toward any architecture, on all detectors and both datasets. Result: AP drops stay at or below about 2.6% everywhere (car drops -0.1% to 1.6%), and confidence barely moves, so the detectors are not fooled by a generic perturbation pattern.

Characterise what kind of error the attacks cause. Setup: compute each detector's mean false positives and false negatives on clean data and the change under each attack on both datasets. Result: the attacks are predominantly erasing, raising false negatives (objects vanish) more than false positives; the transformer-headed voxel detector built to reduce false negatives produces many of them under coordinate shifts, consistent with its global attention spreading noise from distant points into object features.

Compare vulnerability between the sparser and denser dataset. Setup: same detectors and attacks on nuScenes (32-beam) and Waymo (64-beam). Result: for the voxel detectors the car AP drop under coordinate shifts rises from 65.5 to 91.0 (CenterPoint) and 38.9 to 88.5 (FocalFormer3D), and under the feature-space attack from 16.6 to 82.0 and 17.5 to 82.1, whereas point removal hurts the pillar detectors more on the sparser dataset (24.6 and 25.9 on nuScenes vs 2.3 and 17.7 on Waymo). Pillar detectors change little between datasets under coordinate shifts (20.2 vs 18.6, 10.0 vs 9.4).

Test whether nearby objects, which carry more points, are harder to attack. Setup: bin objects by distance from the ego vehicle into near (under 20 m), mid (20-35 m) and far (35-50 m) on both datasets and plot attack success for every detector-attack pair. Result: for most pairs near objects are attacked less successfully, as expected, but under the coordinate-perturbation and feature-space attacks success is roughly the same at all distances.

Relate attack success to per-object point density and to which points are touched. Setup: plot attack success against the number of points inside each object's box after manipulation; and split each object's points into an inner core and an outer shell using a box scaled by 0.8, chosen because it splits points roughly evenly on both datasets, then compare success when attacks act on inner or outer points. Result: some pairs (FocalFormer3D and CenterPoint under coordinate shifts, PointPillars under injection) are vulnerable regardless of density and some show success rising with density (PointPillars and CenterPoint under the feature attack on nuScenes; CenterPoint under injection and PillarNeSt under coordinate shifts on Waymo), while most other pairs become more robust as density rises. Inner and outer perturbations hurt about equally, except that removing core points hurts much more than removing shell points.

dropped: Localisation-error decomposition (scale, yaw, translation; reported only as a figure without numbers); qualitative architectural interpretations.
notes: Analysis paper rather than a method paper; claims are comparative across architectures. The c1 headline mentions point removal only for context; the bar rests on PB/NE drops for voxel detectors.
